name: Functional Diversity and Adaptive Capacity
definition: Functional diversity and adaptive capacity describe the sustainability value of maintaining sufficiently varied components, roles, capabilities or response strategies so that a system can continue functioning, adapt, or recover when conditions change. Diversity matters here because different components may respond differently to the same disturbance, provide complementary functions, or provide alternatives when one pathway fails.
scope: Applies when variation among components has a demonstrable or plausible functional relationship to resilience, adaptation, recovery, or response diversity. The relevant unit of diversity may be biological species, functional traits, technologies, infrastructure pathways, organizations, knowledge sources, or other system components. Diversity is not inherently sustainable: additional components can also increase resource demand, coordination burden, incompatibility, or risk.
core_ideas: Maintain useful variation; preserve functional redundancy where failure is consequential; combine complementary capabilities; avoid unnecessary monocultures or single-path dependencies; assess the cost of diversity against its resilience benefit; distinguish diversity itself from the functions diversity enables.
semantic_description: The principle connects biodiversity and other forms of system diversity to the ability to absorb disturbance, adapt and recover.
keywords_synonyms: biodiversity; diversity; redundancy; resilience; adaptive capacity
sustainability_principle: A system should preserve diversity where diversity provides the variation, redundancy or complementary functions needed to remain resilient under changing conditions.
underlying_mechanism: Diverse components can respond differently to disturbance, reducing the chance that one failure disables the whole system.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Biodiversity and resilient ecological systems; diverse agricultural and social systems.
evidence_status: UN SDG 15; IPCC AR6 sustainability and resilience literature.
transferability: Agriculture; ecology; infrastructure; organizations; data/AI; communities
boundary_conditions: Diversity should not be treated as inherently beneficial if it creates unmanaged hazards or unnecessary complexity.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when the graph contains diversity, redundancy, modularity, biodiversity or resilience concepts; strengthen only when the application context shows functional diversity matters.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Resource Regeneration Capacity
definition: Resource regeneration capacity is the ability of a resource stock, ecological process, or supporting system to replenish or recover at a rate sufficient to sustain an intended pattern of use over the relevant time horizon. Sustainability therefore depends not simply on whether a resource is currently available, but on the relationship between withdrawals or disturbance and the processes and conditions that restore the resource.
scope: Applies primarily to renewable or regenerating resources such as groundwater, surface water, soil fertility, biomass, fisheries, forests, and ecosystem functions. Regeneration may be spatially and seasonally variable and may be reduced by pollution, land-use change, climate change, or excessive extraction. Non-renewable resources require depletion, substitution, recycling, and transition analysis rather than a regeneration-rate test.
core_ideas: Match use to regeneration; protect the processes that enable renewal; distinguish stock from flow; account for spatial and temporal variability; avoid treating short-term availability as evidence of sustainable supply; monitor regeneration and recovery conditions.
semantic_description: The principle connects resource demand with the rate and conditions of renewal rather than short-term availability.
keywords_synonyms: regeneration; sustainable withdrawal; replenishment; resource use; carrying capacity
sustainability_principle: A system that depends on renewal should not use a resource faster than the processes that replenish the resource or the conditions that sustain its renewal.
underlying_mechanism: The sustainable rate of use is constrained by regeneration and supporting ecological processes.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Traditional water allocation; fisheries and forestry management; sustainable groundwater withdrawal.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 6, 12 and 14; FAO sustainability principles; IPCC AR6.
transferability: Water; fisheries; forestry; agriculture; energy; materials
boundary_conditions: Renewal rates vary spatially and temporally; technological substitution does not remove ecological limits.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when resource stocks, flows, recharge, regeneration, extraction or renewal constraints are present; strengthen when the application context contains a measurable renewal rate.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Ecological Function Integration
definition: Ecological function integration recognizes that ecological processes can provide functions that would otherwise require engineered, material, or energy-intensive interventions, while simultaneously supporting ecosystem health. The sustainability opportunity arises when an ecological process is deliberately retained, restored, or incorporated into system design rather than treated only as background environmental context.
scope: Applies only where the ecological process actually performs a relevant function and where its performance, reliability, safety, maintenance requirements, and ecological consequences can be evaluated. Ecological processes should not be treated as interchangeable with engineered systems merely because they provide a superficially similar service.
core_ideas: Use ecological processes as functional system components where appropriate; identify the mechanism of service provision; preserve ecological integrity; compare ecological and engineered alternatives on equivalent functional outcomes; account for variability, maintenance, failure, and co-benefits.
semantic_description: The principle abstracts from cases in which a human system is redesigned to work with an existing ecological interaction.
keywords_synonyms: ecological function; biological control; ecological engineering; nature-based process
sustainability_principle: When natural ecological interactions can safely perform a useful function, human systems should support those interactions rather than unnecessarily replacing them with resource-intensive technical processes.
underlying_mechanism: An organism or ecological relationship performs a function that would otherwise require an external technical input.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Pearl farming using reef fish to control biofouling on culture equipment.
evidence_status: Sustainable Pearls; UN SDG partnership material; marine ecosystem management literature.
transferability: Aquaculture; agriculture; wastewater; landscape management; ecological engineering
boundary_conditions: Do not assume every natural process is beneficial, controllable or appropriate for production.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when an ecological interaction or ecosystem function could plausibly provide a required service; validate against ecological evidence and safety/boundary conditions before recommending.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Local Ecological Fit
definition: Local ecological fit is the principle that sustainability performance depends partly on how well a system's design, operation, materials, timing, and management are matched to the physical, ecological, climatic, hydrological, and social conditions of its place. A technically valid solution can perform poorly when assumptions developed elsewhere do not hold locally.
scope: Applies when local conditions materially influence resource flows, hazards, ecosystem response, user behaviour, maintenance, or system performance. Local adaptation does not imply that locally developed solutions are automatically superior or that standardized technology should be rejected; both must be evaluated against the same functional and sustainability criteria.
core_ideas: Design for place; make local climate and hydrology explicit; account for local ecology and terrain; consider local materials and maintenance capacity; incorporate relevant local knowledge; test whether transferred assumptions remain valid under local boundary conditions.
semantic_description: The principle treats local environmental and social conditions as design inputs rather than external constraints. Distinguishing emphasis: the fit being tested is primarily ecological, hydrological, climatic, hazard, or other place-specific environmental performance.
keywords_synonyms: place-based design; local ecological fit; climate-responsive design; local conditions
sustainability_principle: Human systems should work with local ecological conditions and processes rather than forcing the same design or operating model onto fundamentally different places.
underlying_mechanism: Local conditions determine available resources, natural flows, hazards and appropriate operating regimes.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Traditional irrigation, vernacular architecture, climate-adapted settlements.
evidence_status: UNESCO traditional knowledge/irrigation documentation; FAO; UN SDG Goals 6 and 11.
transferability: Civil engineering; architecture; agriculture; urban planning; water management
boundary_conditions: Local fit must be tested against contemporary population, safety, health and performance requirements.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when site-specific climate, hydrology, ecology, hazards or local operating conditions materially affect design; context evidence should determine relevance.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Seasonal and Cyclical Alignment
definition: Seasonal and cyclical alignment is the practice of matching resource use, system operation, ecological intervention, or demand management to predictable temporal patterns in availability, regeneration, climate, ecological activity, or demand. Aligning timing can reduce peak stress and avoid unnecessary capacity or resource use.
scope: Applies where meaningful seasonal, periodic, diurnal, tidal, biological, agricultural, climatic, or demand cycles exist and can be characterized sufficiently for decision-making. Historical cycles cannot be assumed to remain stationary under climate change or other system transitions; uncertainty and changing cycle characteristics must be considered.
core_ideas: Match demand to availability where feasible; exploit predictable cycles; avoid peak-period ecological or resource stress; design storage or flexibility for mismatch periods; monitor changes in cycle timing and amplitude; distinguish genuine cyclic structure from short-term variability.
semantic_description: The principle treats time as a sustainability variable rather than assuming constant resource availability.
keywords_synonyms: seasonality; cycles; timing; ecological calendar; seasonal allocation
sustainability_principle: Resource systems should respond to seasonal and cyclical variation rather than treating availability, demand or ecological capacity as constant.
underlying_mechanism: Seasonal variation changes resource availability, regeneration and risk.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Traditional irrigation calendars; seasonal fisheries closures; rain-fed agriculture.
evidence_status: FAO; UNESCO traditional knowledge; UN SDG Goals 2, 6 and 14.
transferability: Agriculture; water; fisheries; energy; tourism; urban systems
boundary_conditions: Historical cycles cannot be assumed unchanged under climate change or altered land use.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when the system has seasonal, periodic or cyclical variation in resource availability, demand, regeneration or risk.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Shared Resource Governance
definition: Shared resource responsible management holds that resources used by multiple people, organizations, or jurisdictions remain sustainable only when access, use, monitoring, maintenance, and responsibility are connected through appropriate governance arrangements. responsible management is therefore a relationship between resource condition and the institutions or communities that depend on it.
scope: Applies to shared or common-pool resources and public or collectively managed systems where individual actions can affect resource condition or other users. Governance arrangements must reflect the resource characteristics, user community, legal authority, scale, enforcement capacity, and distribution of rights and responsibilities; no single governance form is universally applicable.
core_ideas: Connect rights with responsibilities; define legitimate users and duties; establish monitoring and feedback; address collective-action problems; maintain accountability; adapt rules when resource conditions change; recognize the role of local knowledge and participation.
semantic_description: The principle connects resource viability with institutions and user participation. Distinguishing emphasis: sustainability depends on governance arrangements linking shared users to rules, monitoring, maintenance, and collective responsibility.
keywords_synonyms: commons; responsible management; collective action; shared resources; community governance
sustainability_principle: A shared resource is more likely to remain viable when those who depend on it also have responsibilities and meaningful roles in maintaining the conditions that sustain it.
underlying_mechanism: Users have information, incentives and responsibilities that can support monitoring and maintenance.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Community irrigation, fisheries and common-resource governance.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 6 and 14; scholarly commons-governance evidence.
transferability: Water; fisheries; forests; campus commons; digital commons
boundary_conditions: Community participation is not automatically effective; rules, power, accountability and ecological conditions matter.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when a shared resource has identifiable users, responsibilities, monitoring or maintenance needs; application context may introduce participation/governance recommendations.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Human–Ecological Coupling
definition: Human–ecological coupling recognizes that human systems and ecological systems can exchange material, energy, information, risks, and benefits, creating feedbacks in which changes in one affect the condition and functioning of the other. Sustainability analysis therefore considers these interactions rather than treating society and ecology as independent externalities.
scope: Applies where human activity materially alters ecological processes or where ecological conditions materially influence health, livelihoods, infrastructure, resource availability, safety, or other human outcomes. The relevant system boundary must capture the feedback pathway and appropriate spatial and temporal scales.
core_ideas: Make human–ecological feedbacks explicit; identify dependencies and impacts in both directions; include ecological conditions in system performance; identify trade-offs and synergies; avoid one-way impact assumptions; analyse coupled-system dynamics.
semantic_description: The principle prevents ecological effects from being treated as external to social or engineering systems.
keywords_synonyms: socio-ecological systems; feedback; coupled systems; environmental governance
sustainability_principle: When people, communities and ecosystems depend on the same resource system, decisions should account for reciprocal effects rather than optimizing one component in isolation.
underlying_mechanism: Feedback connects resource use, ecosystem condition and human outcomes.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Integrated watershed and ecosystem management.
evidence_status: IPCC AR6; UN SDG Goals 6, 11 and 15.
transferability: Water; urban planning; agriculture; climate adaptation; public policy
boundary_conditions: The coupling structure must be evidenced rather than assumed.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when human and ecological components are coupled through resource flows, feedbacks or impacts; validate the specific cross-boundary mechanism.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Reciprocal Resource Responsibility
definition: Reciprocal responsible management links the benefits, access, rights, or services obtained from a shared system with corresponding responsibilities to maintain the conditions that sustain those benefits. Reciprocity does not require equal contributions; it requires that legitimate use and responsibility are connected in a way that is appropriate to roles, capacity, rights, and institutional context.
scope: Applies where users receive continuing benefits from a resource, infrastructure system, ecosystem service, community arrangement, or other shared asset and where their actions can affect its continued functioning. Responsibilities may be differentiated by capacity, contribution, legal status, historical role, or degree of impact.
core_ideas: Link benefit with responsibility; recognize differentiated contributions; maintain accountability for resource condition; support mutual obligation; distinguish reciprocity from simple participation; ensure responsibilities are legitimate and enforceable in context.
semantic_description: The principle connects distribution of benefits with maintenance obligations. Distinguishing emphasis: benefits or access are explicitly linked to proportionate responsibilities for sustaining the shared system; broad governance participation alone is insufficient.
keywords_synonyms: reciprocity; responsible management obligations; resource rights; accountability
sustainability_principle: Those who receive benefits from a shared resource should also contribute, in proportion to legitimate responsibilities, to maintaining the resource and the system that sustains it.
underlying_mechanism: Reciprocal arrangements can align incentives for maintenance and long-term resource viability.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Community water allocation and maintenance arrangements.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 6 and 16; commons-governance scholarship.
transferability: Water; community infrastructure; public resources; digital commons
boundary_conditions: Responsibilities must be legitimate, transparent and proportionate.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when benefits and responsibilities are jointly distributed among users of a shared resource; distinguish reciprocity from participation and from generic governance.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Intergenerational Options
definition: Intergenerational options expresses the sustainability requirement that present decisions should not unnecessarily reduce the ability of future people to meet essential needs, respond to uncertainty, or choose among viable development pathways. The emphasis is on preserving future capability and options, particularly where present actions create long-lived commitments or irreversible losses.
scope: Applies to decisions involving resource depletion, persistent pollution, long-lived infrastructure, cumulative environmental change, technological lock-in, loss of knowledge or ecological function, and other effects whose consequences extend across generations. It does not require preserving every existing condition; justified change is compatible with the principle when future capability is not unnecessarily constrained.
core_ideas: Preserve future choice; identify irreversible and difficult-to-reverse effects; account for long-lived commitments; maintain ecological and institutional capacity; consider cumulative effects; avoid transferring avoidable risks or depleted options to future generations.
semantic_description: Intergenerational sustainability is about preserving future capability, not predicting exactly what future people will want.
keywords_synonyms: intergenerational equity; future generations; long-term options; responsible management
sustainability_principle: Current decisions should preserve the ecological, social and knowledge conditions that allow future generations to meet needs and exercise meaningful choices.
underlying_mechanism: Long-lived decisions can constrain future choices through depletion, lock-in or irreversible damage.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Intergenerational equity in sustainable development.
evidence_status: UN 2030 Agenda; UN SDG 12; UN SDG 13; KPR Intergenerational Equity Principle.
transferability: Infrastructure; energy; water; land use; policy; education
boundary_conditions: Future preferences are uncertain; the principle focuses on preserving capabilities and options.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when a decision has long-lived effects, depletion, lock-in or irreversible consequences that can constrain future choices.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Loss Prevention Before Supply Expansion
definition: Loss prevention before supply expansion prioritizes reducing avoidable losses, leakage, waste, degradation, and unnecessary demand before increasing extraction, production, transport capacity, or external supply. The principle treats the existing system's unproductive losses as a potential source of capacity that can be recovered before additional resource throughput is committed.
scope: Applies where losses or avoidable demand are material, measurable or reasonably estimable and where interventions can reduce them without unacceptable rebound or lifecycle impacts. It is not a universal rule against supply expansion; additional capacity may still be necessary after technically and economically credible loss-prevention opportunities have been evaluated.
core_ideas: Measure losses before adding supply; distinguish technical losses from unavoidable losses; reduce leakage and waste; improve demand management; compare conservation with new supply on equivalent functional outcomes; check rebound and lifecycle effects.
semantic_description: The principle changes the first question from 'How do we supply more?' to 'Why is what we already have insufficient?'. Distinguishing emphasis: the primary recoverable capacity comes from reducing physical or operational losses, leakage, waste, or degradation within the existing system.
keywords_synonyms: loss prevention; demand management; efficiency; sufficiency; avoidable loss
sustainability_principle: Before increasing supply or extracting additional resources, examine whether existing resources are being lost, wasted, degraded or unnecessarily demanded.
underlying_mechanism: Preventing loss can reduce the need for new extraction or capacity.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Food-loss prevention; water leakage reduction; energy-loss reduction.
evidence_status: UN SDG 12.3 and 12.2; UN SDG 6.4; UN SDG 9.1.
transferability: Food; water; energy; infrastructure; manufacturing; data centers
boundary_conditions: Efficiency gains must not create rebound effects or shift burdens elsewhere.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when loss, leakage, waste, avoidable demand or degradation can be quantified before additional supply or extraction is considered.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Residual Resource Value
definition: Residual resource value recognizes that an output, by-product, effluent, heat stream, material residue, biological residue, or information product that has lost value in its original process may still contain usable function or recoverable value in another process. Sustainability improves when technically viable secondary uses are evaluated before residuals are treated as waste.
scope: Applies where a residual has sufficient quality, quantity, timing, location, safety, and compatibility for a secondary use or recovery pathway. Secondary use is not automatically preferable: treatment, transport, contamination risk, additional energy demand, market dependence, and downstream impacts must be included in the assessment.
core_ideas: Look beyond the original process boundary; identify residual function; match residual quality to secondary requirements; prioritize safe recovery and cascading use; assess logistics and lifecycle impacts; distinguish genuine resource recovery from burden shifting.
semantic_description: The principle challenges process boundaries that define outputs as waste without evaluating residual function. Distinguishing emphasis: the concept identifies residual value that may remain in an output or waste stream even before a specific receiving process or exchange partner is established.
keywords_synonyms: by-product; resource recovery; waste-to-resource; cascading use
sustainability_principle: A useful output from one process should be evaluated as a potential input to another process before it is classified as waste and discarded.
underlying_mechanism: A system boundary can hide useful exchanges between processes.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Industrial symbiosis; nutrient recovery; wastewater reuse; food by-product utilization.
evidence_status: UN SDG 12.4 and 12.5; UN SDG Indicator Framework.
transferability: Chemical engineering; civil/environmental engineering; agriculture; manufacturing; campuses
boundary_conditions: Not every waste stream is a safe or viable resource.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when outputs, by-products, residuals or waste streams may have technically defensible value as inputs to another process.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Long-Life Use
definition: Long-life use holds that retaining the useful function of a product, component, facility, infrastructure asset, or system for longer can preserve embodied materials, energy, labour, capital, and knowledge that would otherwise be required for replacement. Longevity is valuable when the retained system continues to deliver the required function safely and efficiently.
scope: Applies when durability and continued use provide a net lifecycle benefit and do not create disproportionate operating energy, maintenance, safety, performance, or adaptation penalties. A longer physical life is not automatically more sustainable if the asset becomes functionally obsolete or imposes large ongoing burdens.
core_ideas: Preserve useful function; design and operate for durability; maintain assets; account for embodied value; compare extension with replacement using lifecycle assessment; distinguish physical longevity from functional relevance.
semantic_description: Sustainability can arise from preserving existing functional value rather than repeatedly creating replacement capacity.
keywords_synonyms: durability; long-life use; maintenance; embodied value; lifecycle
sustainability_principle: Systems should retain useful materials, components and functions for as long as practical before discarding and replacing them.
underlying_mechanism: Maintenance and continued use preserve already invested material, energy, labour and knowledge.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Repair traditions; durable vernacular structures; maintainable infrastructure.
evidence_status: UN SDG 12; lifecycle and sustainable design literature.
transferability: Buildings; infrastructure; equipment; products; software systems
boundary_conditions: Longer life is not automatically better if obsolete systems are unsafe or inefficient.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when durability, maintenance, retained function or asset life is relevant; do not infer repairability unless the context supports it.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Repairability and Life Extension
definition: Repairability and life extension emphasizes restoring useful function through inspection, maintenance, repair, refurbishment, component replacement, or upgrading when this avoids unnecessary disposal and replacement. The sustainability value arises from retaining existing material, manufacturing effort, infrastructure, skills, and functional capability.
scope: Applies when a system can be safely diagnosed and restored to an acceptable performance level and when repair does not create unacceptable reliability, safety, energy, environmental, or economic burdens. Repairability depends on access to parts, tools, information, skills, modularity, standards, and institutional support.
core_ideas: Design for diagnosis and repair; preserve replaceable components; maintain technical information and skills; evaluate repair versus replacement on lifecycle outcomes; include safety and reliability; avoid treating repair as beneficial when continued operation is materially inferior.
semantic_description: The principle makes repair an option to be evaluated before replacement rather than an automatic rule. Distinguishing emphasis: the primary mechanism is retaining an existing product or asset in useful service through repair, reuse, or life extension.
keywords_synonyms: repair; maintainability; repairability; life extension
sustainability_principle: Where a product, structure or system can be safely restored to useful function, repair should be considered before replacement.
underlying_mechanism: Repair restores function while retaining much of the original asset's embodied value.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Traditional craft repair; equipment maintenance; infrastructure rehabilitation.
transferability: Products; infrastructure; equipment; buildings; software
boundary_conditions: Repair can be inappropriate when failure modes, safety or lifecycle impacts make replacement preferable.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when safe restoration of useful function is technically feasible and replacement would discard significant embodied value.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Functional Sufficiency
definition: Functional sufficiency distinguishes the service, capability, or outcome that a person or system actually requires from the quantity of material, energy, space, infrastructure, or throughput used to deliver it. Sustainability can improve when the required function is met with less unnecessary resource demand rather than maximizing output or capacity.
scope: Applies when a meaningful functional requirement can be defined independently of the resource-intensive means used to provide it. Sufficiency does not mean simply reducing consumption regardless of need; essential service levels, safety, accessibility, reliability, and legitimate human requirements must remain satisfied.
core_ideas: Define the required function first; avoid unnecessary demand; separate service from throughput; size systems to actual need; evaluate efficiency and sufficiency together; protect essential access and performance.
semantic_description: The principle separates service provision from resource throughput.
keywords_synonyms: functional requirement; sufficiency; resource demand; efficiency
sustainability_principle: A system should meet its intended human purpose without demanding materially more energy, water, land or other resources than the function requires.
underlying_mechanism: Resource demand should be evaluated against the actual service or capability required.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Efficient buildings, transport, water systems and manufacturing.
transferability: All engineering disciplines; architecture; services; digital systems
boundary_conditions: Efficiency alone can be insufficient if demand keeps expanding or the service definition is wrong.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when the design objective is service/capability delivery and resource demand can be evaluated against the required function rather than output volume alone.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Natural Gradient Utilization
definition: Natural gradient utilization recognizes that naturally occurring gradients and flows—such as gravitational head, pressure differences, temperature differences, solar radiation, wind, or topographic elevation—can sometimes provide part of a required function without continuous external energy input. Sustainable design can exploit these conditions where they are reliable enough for the intended service.
scope: Applies only where the natural gradient is physically available, sufficiently stable or manageable, and compatible with required performance, safety, control, reliability, and environmental conditions. Using a natural gradient does not eliminate embodied energy or other lifecycle impacts and should not be confused with universally passive operation.
core_ideas: Use available environmental gradients; minimize unnecessary pumping or active energy conversion; design around natural flows; account for variability and storage; protect ecological processes; verify that passive or low-energy operation still meets the required function.
semantic_description: The principle encourages designers to treat natural gradients and flows as design resources.
keywords_synonyms: gravity; passive design; natural flow; gradient; passive environmental control
sustainability_principle: Where natural gradients, flows or environmental conditions can safely provide part of a required function, design should consider using them before adding active energy or material inputs.
underlying_mechanism: A natural potential difference or environmental condition performs part of the required work.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Qanat/aflaj gravity conveyance; passive cooling and ventilation.
evidence_status: UNESCO traditional water systems; sustainable building literature.
transferability: Water; buildings; drainage; energy; transport
boundary_conditions: Natural systems are site-specific and may not meet reliability or capacity requirements alone.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when natural head, pressure, temperature difference, gravity, airflow or another environmental gradient can safely perform part of the required function.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Distributed Resilience
definition: Distributed resilience describes the capacity gained when critical functions are supported by multiple geographically, functionally, or organizationally distributed components or pathways rather than depending on a single point of failure. Distribution can allow local continuation of service when part of a system is disrupted.
scope: Applies when failure of centralized components, networks, facilities, supply chains, or decision points could create unacceptable consequences and when distributed alternatives can maintain essential function. Distribution can also increase coordination, maintenance, cybersecurity, interoperability, and lifecycle burdens; these trade-offs must be evaluated.
core_ideas: Reduce critical single points of failure; distribute capacity where justified; retain local capability; design for graceful degradation; assess coordination costs; distinguish redundancy that improves resilience from duplication that merely increases resource use.
semantic_description: Resilience can be increased by distributing critical functions and decision points.
keywords_synonyms: distributed resilience; redundancy; decentralization; fault tolerance
sustainability_principle: Critical functions should not depend unnecessarily on a single resource, component, pathway or decision point when distributed alternatives can provide greater resilience.
underlying_mechanism: Distributed systems can continue partial operation when one component fails.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Distributed water storage; decentralized energy; distributed computing.
evidence_status: Engineering resilience literature; UN SDG 9 and 11.
transferability: Power; water; ICT; infrastructure; health; communities
boundary_conditions: Distribution is not automatically more resilient; interconnection and governance can create new vulnerabilities.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when critical service continuity can benefit from distributed resources, pathways, components or decision points; test failure modes and trade-offs.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Ecological Infrastructure
definition: Ecological infrastructure treats ecological processes, habitats, vegetation, soils, wetlands, waterways, and other ecosystem structures as components that can contribute to human and environmental functions alongside or in combination with conventional infrastructure. The principle emphasizes multifunctional infrastructure that maintains or restores ecological processes while meeting its intended service.
scope: Applies where ecological components can provide measurable functions such as water retention, filtration, cooling, erosion control, habitat, flood attenuation, or connectivity. Ecological infrastructure must be assessed for performance variability, land requirements, maintenance, hazards, time to maturity, and compatibility with the primary service.
core_ideas: Integrate ecological function into infrastructure design; pursue multifunctionality; protect and restore ecosystem processes; combine grey and ecological infrastructure where appropriate; measure both service and ecological outcomes; design for long-term maintenance.
semantic_description: The principle shifts infrastructure evaluation from damage minimization alone toward potential ecological contribution. Distinguishing emphasis: ecological processes or structures perform an infrastructure-like service alongside or instead of conventional infrastructure.
keywords_synonyms: ecological infrastructure; multifunctional infrastructure; nature-positive design
sustainability_principle: Infrastructure should be evaluated not only for the service it provides to people but also for ecological functions that its location and design can preserve, restore or create.
underlying_mechanism: Infrastructure occupies physical space and can alter flows, habitat and microclimate; design can intentionally shape these effects.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Green infrastructure; constructed wetlands; habitat-integrated infrastructure.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 6, 11 and 15; nature-based solutions literature.
transferability: Civil; architecture; urban planning; water; transport
boundary_conditions: Ecological claims require evidence; 'green' appearance is not sufficient.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when infrastructure interacts materially with habitat, water, microclimate or ecological processes and can be designed for multiple functions.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Nature-Positive Occupied Space
definition: Nature-positive occupied space proposes that land, buildings, campuses, transport corridors, and other developed spaces should be evaluated not only by the human functions they accommodate but also by whether their occupied footprint can retain, restore, or create measurable ecological functions. The objective is to reduce the ecological loss associated with development and, where feasible, produce net ecological gains.
scope: Applies at the site and landscape scale where design and management can influence habitat, biodiversity, water retention, soil function, thermal regulation, connectivity, or ecological resources. A planted or green surface is not automatically nature-positive; ecological quality, additionality, permanence, maintenance, and displacement effects must be assessed.
core_ideas: Treat occupied space as multifunctional; retain ecological structure where possible; restore habitat and ecological processes; connect fragmented habitat; manage water and heat through ecological functions; verify ecological outcomes rather than relying on labels.
semantic_description: A stronger form of nature-positive design that asks what ecological function can be created in the same footprint. Distinguishing emphasis: the occupied or developed footprint is evaluated for measurable ecological retention, restoration, or net gain, even when ecological function is not replacing an infrastructure service.
keywords_synonyms: nature-positive infrastructure; ecological function; multifunctionality
sustainability_principle: A system that occupies ecological space should seek opportunities to provide, rather than merely avoid damaging, ecological functions.
underlying_mechanism: The occupied footprint becomes an opportunity for habitat, water retention, cooling, carbon or other functions.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Green roofs, constructed wetlands, bioswales, habitat-integrated structures.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 11 and 15; emerging nature-positive design literature.
transferability: Buildings; roads; campuses; cities; industrial sites
boundary_conditions: Ecological function must be defined, measured and maintained.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when occupied or developed space can support additional ecological functions without compromising the primary service or creating material hazards.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Ecological Limits
definition: Ecological limits recognizes that human systems operate within biophysical conditions and ecosystem capacities that cannot be removed simply by technological substitution or economic optimization. Some ecological functions, thresholds, stocks, and feedbacks constrain what levels of extraction, pollution, disturbance, or transformation can be sustained.
scope: Applies when system performance depends materially on ecological stocks, flows, thresholds, carrying capacity, assimilative capacity, biodiversity, climate stability, or other biophysical conditions. Limits are context- and scale-dependent and should be supported by evidence; the principle does not imply that every ecological state has a single fixed threshold.
core_ideas: Identify ecological dependencies and constraints; distinguish physical limits from assumed limits; detect thresholds and nonlinear feedbacks; avoid unlimited substitution assumptions; keep system demand within defensible ecological conditions; monitor conditions that could change the limit.
semantic_description: The principle distinguishes technological mitigation from the continued functioning of life-support systems.
keywords_synonyms: ecological limits; thresholds; substitution; planetary boundaries
sustainability_principle: Development should be adapted to ecological limits and system capacity rather than assuming that technology can indefinitely substitute for degraded natural functions.
underlying_mechanism: Natural systems provide functions that may be difficult, costly or impossible to fully replace.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Climate adaptation, water management, biodiversity protection.
evidence_status: IPCC AR6; UN SDG Goals 6, 13 and 15.
transferability: All fields involving resource or ecological dependencies
boundary_conditions: Limits are context-specific and should be supported by evidence rather than vague claims.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when a system depends on ecological capacity, natural limits or ecosystem functions that are not fully replaceable by technical substitution.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Burden Transfer
definition: Burden transfer identifies situations in which an apparent sustainability improvement in one location, group, lifecycle stage, environmental compartment, or time period is achieved by shifting costs, risks, emissions, resource depletion, or health and social burdens elsewhere. A sustainability claim is incomplete when its relevant burden transfers are outside the assessment boundary.
scope: Applies whenever an intervention changes material or energy flows, production location, waste destination, labour conditions, exposure, resource sourcing, or timing of impacts. The appropriate boundary should include materially affected actors and lifecycle stages without expanding the analysis so broadly that causal relevance is lost.
core_ideas: Check where burdens go; use lifecycle and supply-chain perspectives; examine distributional effects; identify temporal transfers; avoid double counting; distinguish genuine burden reduction from relocation or delayed realization.
semantic_description: Sustainability assessment should track where benefits and burdens go, not only whether one local metric improves.
keywords_synonyms: burden shifting; externalities; lifecycle; system boundary; trade-offs
sustainability_principle: When solving a problem, evaluate whether the proposed solution transfers the environmental, social or health burden to another place, group, life stage or future time.
underlying_mechanism: A solution changes flows or risks across boundaries.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Lifecycle assessment; pollution displacement; outsourcing of hazardous work.
evidence_status: UN SDG 12; UN SDG 10; IPCC lifecycle and equity literature.
transferability: Engineering; business; policy; supply chains; urban systems
boundary_conditions: Not every upstream/downstream effect is equally material; prioritization is required.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when an intervention may relocate environmental, health, social or temporal burdens; require explicit boundary and affected-party analysis.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Equitable Sustainability
definition: Equitable sustainability holds that sustainability outcomes include the distribution of benefits, burdens, risks, opportunities, access, and decision-making power among people and groups. A technically or environmentally effective intervention can still be unsustainable in social terms when it systematically concentrates burdens or excludes affected populations from relevant benefits or opportunities.
scope: Applies where environmental or technological decisions have differentiated effects because of income, vulnerability, geography, access, institutional power, disability, age, occupation, or other contextually relevant factors. Equity analysis must be evidence-based and should not infer vulnerability solely from group labels.
core_ideas: Examine distribution, not only aggregate performance; identify disproportionately affected groups; protect essential access; assess affordability and exposure; consider procedural as well as distributive equity; make trade-offs visible.
semantic_description: The principle prevents aggregate improvement from hiding systematic harm to less powerful groups.
keywords_synonyms: environmental justice; equity; distribution; vulnerability; fairness
sustainability_principle: A sustainability intervention should improve or protect human wellbeing without requiring another population or community to bear disproportionate costs or risks.
underlying_mechanism: Benefits and burdens are socially distributed rather than experienced equally.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Environmental justice; equitable public-service design.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goal 10; UN 2030 Agenda; IPCC AR6 equity literature.
transferability: Infrastructure; health; environment; policy; technology
boundary_conditions: Equity does not always mean identical outcomes; the relevant distribution must be defined.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when benefits, costs, risks or access are unevenly distributed across populations; use application evidence rather than discipline alone.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Human Capability and Dignity
definition: Human capability and dignity frames sustainability in terms of whether systems expand or constrain people's substantive ability to live healthy, secure, meaningful, autonomous, and socially valued lives. It shifts attention from aggregate production or consumption alone toward the capabilities, freedoms, access, agency, and conditions through which people can achieve valued outcomes.
scope: Applies to technologies, infrastructure, institutions, services, workplaces, education, health systems, and policies that materially affect human opportunity or wellbeing. Capability should be operationalized through context-specific outcomes; the principle does not imply that all preferences or increases in consumption automatically represent improved wellbeing.
core_ideas: Protect dignity and agency; expand meaningful capabilities; ensure access to essential services; distinguish output from human outcome; identify constraints on autonomy and opportunity; assess who gains or loses capability.
semantic_description: The principle places people as ends of development rather than only inputs or consumers.
keywords_synonyms: human wellbeing; dignity; capability; human development; agency
sustainability_principle: Systems intended to serve people should be designed around human needs, dignity and capabilities rather than treating people primarily as consumers, inputs or units of economic output.
underlying_mechanism: Human outcomes are broader than income, consumption or productivity.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Human development and capability approaches; rights-based design.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 3, 4 and 10; UN 2030 Agenda.
transferability: Health; education; engineering; economics; policy; technology
boundary_conditions: Capability is context-dependent and must be defined with affected people.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when a system materially affects human capability, dignity, autonomy, access or wellbeing; evaluate people as affected agents rather than only demand units.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Preventive Sustainability
definition: Preventive sustainability prioritizes changing upstream causes of avoidable harm when credible evidence shows that prevention can reduce the probability, magnitude, or recurrence of environmental, health, safety, or social damage. It favors interventions that alter causal conditions rather than repeatedly managing consequences after harm has occurred.
scope: Applies when the causal pathway to a material harm is sufficiently understood and preventive intervention is feasible and proportionate. Prevention is distinct from treatment, mitigation, compensation, and emergency response, although these may remain necessary where prevention cannot eliminate risk.
core_ideas: Identify causes before symptoms; intervene upstream; reduce exposure and hazard at source; compare prevention with downstream control; account for residual risk; evaluate whether prevention creates new burdens.
semantic_description: The principle moves intervention upstream from response to prevention. Distinguishing emphasis: use this concept for broad proactive avoidance of sustainability harm across design or operations, rather than for the narrower sequence of preventing pollution or damage before remediation.
keywords_synonyms: prevention; risk reduction; upstream intervention; public health
sustainability_principle: Where preventable harm can be reduced by changing the conditions that produce it, prevention should be considered before relying primarily on intervention after harm occurs.
underlying_mechanism: Removing or reducing causal conditions can reduce recurring harm and associated resource demand.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Public-health prevention; occupational safety; pollution prevention.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goal 3; UN SDG Goal 8; IPCC risk-management literature.
transferability: Health; workplace; environmental engineering; infrastructure; policy
boundary_conditions: Prevention is not always possible; residual response capacity remains necessary.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when causal conditions of avoidable harm can be changed upstream; distinguish prevention from downstream mitigation or treatment.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Care and Dependency
definition: Care and dependency recognizes that human wellbeing depends on relationships and systems of care throughout the life course and during periods of illness, disability, ageing, childhood, crisis, or other dependency. Sustainable systems therefore need to accommodate care needs, accessibility, caregiver capacity, and the unequal distribution of care work.
scope: Applies wherever system design, infrastructure, employment, public services, technology, or policy affects people whose ability to act independently is limited or temporarily reduced. Dependency is context-specific and should not be equated with incapacity or reduced human value.
core_ideas: Design for accessibility and care; recognize dependency as a normal life-course condition; support caregivers; reduce avoidable care burdens; maintain continuity of essential support; evaluate whether system design excludes people with different capabilities.
semantic_description: The principle broadens sustainability beyond autonomous economic actors.
keywords_synonyms: care; dependency; vulnerability; life course; social care
sustainability_principle: Systems of care should recognize dependency and vulnerability as normal features of human life rather than treating care as an external or residual activity.
underlying_mechanism: Human wellbeing depends on care relationships and supportive institutions.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Care systems; accessible infrastructure; public health and social support.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 3, 5 and 10; human-development literature.
transferability: Healthcare; architecture; transport; education; workplaces; public policy
boundary_conditions: Care arrangements differ culturally and institutionally; avoid assuming one model.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when system performance depends on care, dependency, accessibility or vulnerability; include affected human needs in the application context.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Social Cohesion and Mutual Support
definition: Social cohesion and mutual support concerns the relationships, trust, networks, shared norms, and cooperative capacities that enable people and organizations to coordinate, assist one another, resolve disputes, and respond collectively to disturbance. These social capacities can influence whether technical or institutional interventions function in practice.
scope: Applies when cooperation, trust, information exchange, mutual aid, collective response, or conflict resolution materially affects system performance or resilience. Social cohesion should not be equated with uniformity or absence of disagreement; legitimate disagreement, deliberation, and institutional conflict resolution can strengthen a system.
core_ideas: Build trustworthy relationships; preserve communication networks; enable mutual aid; support constructive conflict resolution; recognize social networks as system capacity; avoid assuming cohesion where evidence of cooperation is absent.
semantic_description: The principle treats social relationships as part of the conditions enabling collective resilience.
keywords_synonyms: social networks; trust; cooperation; social cohesion; prosocial behaviour
sustainability_principle: A sustainable society should preserve the relationships, trust and mutual support that enable people to cooperate through ordinary needs and periods of stress.
underlying_mechanism: Social connections influence information flow, cooperation and collective response.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Community networks; mutual-aid systems; participatory institutions.
transferability: Communities; organizations; campuses; governance; digital platforms
boundary_conditions: Social cohesion can also exclude outsiders; inclusion and rights must be considered.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when cooperation, trust, mutual support or social networks materially affect system functioning or response under stress.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Meaningful Participation
definition: Meaningful participation requires that people materially affected by a decision have an appropriate opportunity to contribute relevant knowledge, identify impacts, question assumptions, deliberate alternatives, and influence the decision or its implementation. Participation is substantive when input has a credible pathway into decision-making rather than serving only as information collection or symbolic consultation.
scope: Applies when affected people possess relevant experience, local knowledge, interests, rights, or decision-making roles and when participation can improve legitimacy, information quality, implementation, or distributional outcomes. The form and depth of participation should be proportionate to the decision and institutional context.
core_ideas: Identify affected actors; provide accessible opportunities to participate; make decision influence explicit; incorporate relevant local knowledge; provide feedback on how input was used; distinguish consultation, participation, co-design, and delegated decision-making.
semantic_description: The principle connects knowledge quality and legitimacy with participation. Distinguishing emphasis: the core requirement is genuine stakeholder influence on information, priorities, or decisions; the setting need not involve governance of a shared natural resource.
keywords_synonyms: participation; stakeholder engagement; local knowledge; procedural justice
sustainability_principle: People affected by a decision should have meaningful opportunities to contribute knowledge, question assumptions and influence the decision where their interests are materially affected.
underlying_mechanism: Affected people possess context and interests not always visible to technical decision-makers.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Community planning; environmental assessment; participatory design.
transferability: Engineering; planning; law; policy; public services; research
boundary_conditions: Participation cannot replace technical expertise; it must interact with evidence and professional responsibility.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when affected people hold relevant local knowledge, interests or decision rights; participation must be meaningful to the decision at issue.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Mechanism-Based Traditional Knowledge
definition: Mechanism-based traditional knowledge examines historical, Indigenous, local, or community-held practices by identifying the physical, ecological, social, or organizational mechanisms that allowed a practice to function before judging whether the practice remains appropriate. The principle supports critical learning from accumulated experience without treating age or cultural origin as proof of sustainability.
scope: Applies when a practice contains potentially transferable knowledge about local materials, climate, ecology, resource management, construction, agriculture, health, water, or social organization. Knowledge must be interpreted with attention to provenance, cultural rights, context, changing conditions, evidence, and the possibility that some practices may no longer be appropriate.
core_ideas: Ask how the practice works; preserve relevant knowledge and attribution; test mechanisms under current conditions; distinguish transferable mechanism from historical form; respect knowledge holders and cultural context; combine local evidence with scientific validation where appropriate.
semantic_description: The principle turns traditional practice into a source of testable hypotheses rather than nostalgia.
keywords_synonyms: traditional knowledge; local knowledge; historical practice; mechanism recovery
sustainability_principle: Knowledge that has enabled a community to live with a particular place should be examined for its underlying mechanisms before being discarded as obsolete.
underlying_mechanism: Long-term local observation may contain system knowledge that is absent from generic models.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Traditional irrigation, seed systems, vernacular architecture and local ecological knowledge.
evidence_status: UNESCO; FAO; IPCC recognition of Indigenous and local knowledge.
transferability: All disciplines; especially engineering, agriculture, water and architecture
boundary_conditions: Historical persistence alone is not evidence of sustainability or suitability today.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when place-based or community-held knowledge may contain mechanisms relevant to the technical problem; validate the mechanism rather than treating tradition as proof.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Transition Function Preservation
definition: Transition function preservation holds that replacing an existing technology, practice, institution, or infrastructure can unintentionally remove functions that were not represented in the primary performance metric. A transition should therefore compare the full set of material, ecological, social, cultural, maintenance, knowledge, and resilience functions provided by the existing arrangement against those provided by the proposed replacement.
scope: Applies to technology transitions, infrastructure replacement, organizational change, modernization, digitization, and policy reform where the existing system performs multiple explicit or implicit functions. The principle does not oppose replacement; it requires that material functions and dependencies are identified before they are lost.
core_ideas: Inventory existing functions; identify hidden or secondary functions; compare old and new systems on a common functional basis; protect critical functions during transition; provide substitutes where necessary; distinguish obsolete form from valuable function.
semantic_description: The principle asks what the old system was doing beyond the function for which it was explicitly measured.
keywords_synonyms: technology transition; hidden functions; path dependence; functional comparison
sustainability_principle: When a long-used practice is replaced by a modern system, evaluate not only immediate efficiency but also ecological, social, cultural and knowledge functions that may have been lost.
underlying_mechanism: A system can contain tacit functions not represented in performance metrics.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Replacement of traditional water, agricultural, building or craft systems.
evidence_status: Case-based sustainability transition literature; UNESCO/FAO documentation.
transferability: Technology transitions; infrastructure; agriculture; architecture; policy
boundary_conditions: Losses must be demonstrated; do not assume the older system was better.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when replacing an established practice may remove ecological, social, cultural, maintenance or knowledge functions not represented in the primary performance metric.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Adaptive Learning
definition: Adaptive learning treats monitoring, feedback, evaluation, and revision as continuing components of sustainability management under uncertainty and changing conditions. Rather than assuming that an initial design or policy will remain optimal, the system retains the capability to learn from observed outcomes and adjust decisions.
scope: Applies when conditions, system responses, knowledge, or forecasts are uncertain or changing and when decisions can be revised without unacceptable delay or irreversible commitment. Adaptive learning requires meaningful indicators, feedback pathways, decision authority, and institutional capacity to act on evidence.
core_ideas: Monitor outcomes; compare observations with expectations; learn from deviations and failures; update assumptions; revise interventions; preserve flexibility; distinguish genuine adaptive management from repeated changes without learning or evaluation.
semantic_description: Adaptability is treated as a system capability rather than a one-time design property. Distinguishing emphasis: monitoring and feedback are used to learn and revise understanding or practice over time; explicit management of a highly uncertain intervention is not required.
keywords_synonyms: adaptive management; learning; feedback; uncertainty; resilience
sustainability_principle: A system facing uncertainty should preserve the ability to learn, adapt and revise its rules rather than optimizing permanently for conditions that may no longer hold.
underlying_mechanism: Feedback updates decisions as evidence changes.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Adaptive water management; climate adaptation; iterative policy.
evidence_status: IPCC AR6; UN SDG 13; adaptive-management literature.
transferability: Water; climate; infrastructure; governance; AI; organizations
boundary_conditions: Adaptation requires institutional capacity and reliable monitoring.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when feedback, uncertainty and changing conditions require learning and revision rather than one-time optimization.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Precaution Under Irreversible Risk
definition: Precaution under irreversible risk states that when an activity presents a credible possibility of serious or irreversible harm and scientific uncertainty prevents reliable prediction of the outcome, decision-making should avoid unnecessary commitment to the harmful pathway and consider proportionate protective alternatives. Precaution concerns uncertainty combined with consequence, not uncertainty alone.
scope: Applies when potential harm is serious, persistent or difficult to reverse and the evidence is insufficient for confident risk quantification. The principle does not justify arbitrary action: severity, plausibility, uncertainty, proportionality, available alternatives, evidence quality, and the costs of precautionary measures should be considered explicitly.
core_ideas: Identify irreversible outcomes; characterize uncertainty; avoid irreversible lock-in where reasonable; prefer reversible or safer pathways when justified; seek additional evidence; use proportionate safeguards; distinguish precaution from prohibition without evidence.
semantic_description: The principle is not zero-risk; it changes the burden and timing of decision-making under serious uncertainty. Distinguishing emphasis: uncertainty is combined with credible serious or irreversible harm, so protective action may be required before learning-by-doing is acceptable.
keywords_synonyms: precaution; uncertainty; irreversible harm; risk governance
sustainability_principle: Where uncertainty is high and potential harm is serious or irreversible, decisions should avoid locking the system into damaging pathways before critical uncertainties are resolved.
underlying_mechanism: Precaution is triggered by uncertainty plus potentially serious or irreversible harm.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Environmental impact assessment; emerging technology risk assessment.
evidence_status: UN Rio/precautionary principle; UN SDG environmental governance; IPCC risk literature.
transferability: Environmental engineering; law; technology; public policy
boundary_conditions: Precaution must not be used to ignore proportionality, evidence or feasible alternatives.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when uncertainty combines with potentially serious or irreversible harm; apply only where the risk and uncertainty conditions are evidenced.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Cross-Boundary Resource Exchange
domain: Industrial Ecology; Systems Engineering; Urban Systems
definition: Cross-boundary resource exchange identifies sustainability opportunities that become visible when two or more processes, organizations, infrastructures, or ecosystems are analysed as interacting systems and their exchanges of materials, energy, water, information, services, or capacity are made explicit. The principle challenges boundaries that classify a useful exchange as unrelated waste or externality.
scope: Applies when there is a real exchange pathway with compatible quantities, quality, timing, location, ownership, safety, or governance conditions. Expanding a system boundary should improve causal understanding rather than simply aggregate unrelated processes, and the assessment must avoid double counting benefits or impacts.
core_ideas: Map flows across organizational or process boundaries; identify compatible exchanges; test quantity, quality and timing; evaluate transaction and infrastructure requirements; account for lifecycle effects; verify that an apparent exchange creates a net sustainability benefit.
semantic_description: The principle turns boundary selection into an explicit sustainability design decision. Distinguishing emphasis: changing the analytical boundary reveals meaningful resource, energy, water, information, service, or capacity exchanges; a by-product substitution transaction is only one possible form.
keywords_synonyms: system boundary; industrial symbiosis; resource exchange; coupled processes
sustainability_principle: When two systems exchange resources, impacts or services, sustainability should be evaluated across their combined boundary rather than optimizing each independently.
underlying_mechanism: A combined boundary can expose by-product, heat, water, data or infrastructure exchanges.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Industrial symbiosis; campus resource exchange; urban metabolism.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goal 12; industrial ecology literature.
transferability: Chemical; civil; mechanical; energy; campus; urban planning
boundary_conditions: Boundary expansion should be justified by real dependencies, not used to hide impacts.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when two processes, systems or actors exchange materials, energy, water, information, services or infrastructure and the combined boundary changes the sustainability assessment.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Continued Value Under Change
definition: Continued value under change describes the ability of a product, infrastructure system, digital asset, institution, or body of knowledge to retain useful function when conditions such as use, ownership, technology, standards, demand, or operating environment change. Sustainability can improve when systems are designed so that change does not immediately strand valuable components or knowledge.
scope: Applies where future change is plausible and where modularity, interoperability, adaptability, reconfiguration, reuse, or transferable knowledge can preserve function. Flexibility can itself create material, coordination, or complexity costs, so it should be proportionate to credible future uncertainty.
core_ideas: Design for change; preserve interoperability; use modular components where justified; enable reconfiguration and reuse; maintain transferable information; avoid unnecessary lock-in; evaluate flexibility against its lifecycle and complexity costs.
semantic_description: The principle extends durability from physical life to continued functional relevance.
keywords_synonyms: adaptability; modularity; interoperability; future-proofing; reuse
sustainability_principle: A system should be designed so that useful outputs, components or knowledge can remain valuable when the original use, owner, technology or operating condition changes.
underlying_mechanism: Design flexibility preserves value across changing conditions.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Modular buildings; interoperable digital systems; adaptable infrastructure.
evidence_status: Sustainable design and resilience literature; UN SDG 9.
transferability: Infrastructure; software; buildings; products; campuses
boundary_conditions: Flexibility can increase initial complexity and embodied resources; trade-offs must be assessed.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when future changes in use, ownership, technology or operating conditions could otherwise strand useful outputs, components or knowledge.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Metric-Aware Optimization
definition: Metric-aware optimization recognizes that an optimization result is only as sustainable as the objective, constraints, system boundary, and metrics used to produce it. Improving a measurable proxy can worsen important environmental, social, human, or long-term outcomes when those outcomes are omitted or poorly represented.
scope: Applies to engineering optimization, operations research, AI and machine learning, policy metrics, performance management, and multi-objective decision-making. The principle is especially relevant when a metric is a proxy rather than the final outcome of interest or when optimization changes behaviour in response to the metric.
core_ideas: Define the real outcome; distinguish proxy from objective; identify omitted externalities; include material constraints; test for gaming and rebound effects; use supplementary indicators where a single metric is inadequate; examine distributional and long-term consequences.
semantic_description: The principle connects optimization with measurement validity and system boundaries.
keywords_synonyms: optimization; proxy metric; externality; unintended consequence; multi-objective
sustainability_principle: When a system is optimized for a single measurable objective, its sustainability should also be tested against important outcomes that the objective does not measure.
underlying_mechanism: A metric is a proxy for a broader objective; optimizing the proxy can distort the broader outcome.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Algorithmic optimization; engineering design; public-service metrics.
evidence_status: UN SDG 12; measurement and systems literature.
transferability: AI; operations; engineering; policy; economics
boundary_conditions: Not every unmeasured outcome is material; relevance must be justified.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when optimization relies on a proxy metric that may omit important environmental, social, human or long-term outcomes.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Technology for Expanded Human and Ecological Options
definition: Technology for expanded human and ecological options considers technology as a mechanism that changes what actions are feasible, affordable, observable, or scalable. Sustainability therefore asks not only whether a technology is more efficient, but whether the new capability expands the set of desirable options, changes system direction, redistributes capability, or merely accelerates an existing unsustainable pattern.
scope: Applies to digital systems, AI, biotechnology, automation, sensing, advanced materials, energy technologies, and other innovations that materially change system capabilities. Assessment should include access, governance, rebound effects, second-order consequences, dependency, failure modes, and ecological and social impacts.
core_ideas: Evaluate changed option space; distinguish capability expansion from throughput acceleration; examine who gains capability; assess rebound and second-order effects; preserve human and ecological agency; govern new capabilities in proportion to risk.
semantic_description: The principle evaluates innovation by what futures it enables, not merely by efficiency gains.
keywords_synonyms: technology and society; innovation; option space; rebound effects
sustainability_principle: Technological capability should expand human and ecological options rather than simply accelerate an existing unsustainable pattern.
underlying_mechanism: New technology changes what can be observed, controlled or coordinated; its sustainability depends on direction and governance.
derived_from_practice_or_system: AI-enabled monitoring; distributed sensing; assistive technologies; ecological restoration technologies.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 9, 10 and 4.7; emerging technology literature.
transferability: AI; robotics; biotechnology; digital infrastructure; assistive technology
boundary_conditions: Technology can widen or narrow access; sustainability must include distribution and governance.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when technology changes the feasible set of human or ecological actions; evaluate whether the new capability expands sustainable options or merely accelerates an existing pattern.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Human–Ecological Computational Coordination
definition: Human–ecological computational coordination describes the use of sensing, data, models, computation, and feedback systems to represent and coordinate interactions among human activities and ecological conditions. Its sustainability value depends on whether computational objectives adequately represent relevant system outcomes and whether the resulting decisions are interpretable, accountable, and adaptable.
scope: Applies to cyber-physical systems, environmental informatics, AI, digital twins, monitoring networks, decision-support systems, and other computational systems that influence resource or ecological management. Valid measurements, uncertainty characterization, appropriate spatial and temporal scales, governance, privacy where relevant, and clear decision authority are required.
core_ideas: Sense relevant conditions; integrate heterogeneous evidence; model coupled processes; expose feedback; coordinate decisions; represent uncertainty; align computational objectives with human and ecological outcomes; maintain accountability for automated or data-informed decisions.
semantic_description: The principle connects digital capability with sustainability only when data are valid and objectives represent the system that matters.
keywords_synonyms: AI for sustainability; sensing; digital twins; ecological monitoring; decision support
sustainability_principle: Data and computation should be used to make system conditions visible and coordinate action with ecological and human needs, not only to maximize a predefined operational metric.
underlying_mechanism: Digital systems create feedback and coordination capabilities; measurement and objective design determine whether those capabilities help sustainability.
derived_from_practice_or_system: Smart water management; ecological monitoring; energy coordination; health decision support.
evidence_status: UN SDG Goals 9, 11 and 13; UN SDG indicator metadata; AI/sustainability literature.
transferability: AI; IoT; CPS; digital twins; environmental monitoring; public services
boundary_conditions: Bad data, biased objectives or opaque decision rules can worsen outcomes.
recommendation_trigger: Candidate discovery when sensing, data or computation can expose system conditions and coordinate action across human and ecological needs; validate objectives and governance before recommending.
:LABEL: SustainabilityConcept

name: Multi-Future Robustness
definition: Multi-future robustness emphasizes maintaining acceptable performance across a range of plausible future conditions rather than optimizing solely for one predicted future. A robust design or policy retains useful function when climate, demand, resource availability, technology, regulation, or social conditions differ from the planning assumptions.
scope: Applies where future uncertainty is material and where decisions have long lifetimes or high switching costs. Scenario sets should represent meaningful uncertainty rather than arbitrary extremes, and robustness should be evaluated against explicit performance thresholds and decision objectives.
core_ideas: Use multiple plausible futures; identify vulnerabilities across scenarios; prefer solutions that avoid catastrophic underperformance; retain adaptive options; compare robustness with cost; distinguish robustness from simple overdesign.
semantic_description: The principle changes design from prediction optimization to robustness across uncertainty.
keywords_synonyms: foresight; scenarios; robustness; adaptive capacity; uncertainty
sustainability_principle: A future-facing system should be evaluated for how well it can adapt to several plausible futures rather than how efficiently it performs under one predicted future.
underlying_mechanism: Scenario analysis exposes assumptions that single forecasts hide.
